articles.title: This Is the Real History Behind S’mores—And How They Became One of America’s Favorite Treats
articles.content:
## 火焰圣殿：面包干、巧克力与棉花糖的完美组合
如果评选“甜点名人堂”，棉花糖火焰必定首批入选。它们黏糊糊的，吃起来毫无风度可言，却能让人在夏夜后院篝火前或秋日黄昏火堆旁同样感受到魔法般的美味。然而，作为许多人童年回忆和露营夜晚的必备甜点，多数人却不知它的真正起源。

### 从阵地手册到全国风靡
最早的棉花糖火焰配方出现在1927年《女童军徒步与探险指南》中，这一手册旨在帮助团队领袖组织露营和户外活动。配方最初名为“再来一个”（Some More），恰如其分地反映了人们难以停嘴的特性。指南将功劳归于Loretta Scott Crew，她在火堆旁为女童军烤制了这款甜点。

原始配方简单得令人惊艳：将两块棉花糖在炭火上烤至金黄色，夹在饼干和巧克力条中间。棉花糖的余热会让巧克力微微融化。虽然“再来一个”好吃得让人忍不住多吃，但实际上一个就足够了——这一建议如今看来未免过于乐观。

### 从小众到爆款
就像最佳潮流，棉花糖火焰并非一夜爆红，而是逐渐兴起。1927年的女童军手册让这一配方传遍全国，但真正让其成为全国热潮的是二战后的露营热潮。20世纪40至50年代，家庭开始热衷于公路旅行、国家公园游览、夏令营和后院烧烤，数以百万计的美国人开始在篝火旁度过夜晚，手边恰好有着这三种必备食材。

包装好的饼干、棉花糖和巧克力条的流行也让这款甜点变得更易重现。赫舍、克拉夫等公司将这些食材推广为露营必备品，而夏令营则培养了一代又一代的棉花糖火焰爱好者。到20世纪末，棉花糖火焰已不仅仅是一道食谱，更成为美国传统。

### 超越露营的美味革命
赫舍最新的《棉花糖火焰热议报告》显示，如今每年有超过250万美国人享用这款甜点。从简单的篝火小吃演变为全面的风味现象，它激发了从谷物、派饼到饼干、冰淇淋、咖啡伴奶和棉花糖巧克力慕斯等各类产品的创新。

尽管棉花糖火焰已成为经典，但巧克力与棉花糖的搭配并非全新概念。1913年，纳比斯科推出“马洛玛”巧克力饼干，结合了饼干底和蓬松棉花糖，与棉花糖火焰的风味极为相似。最大的不同在于，这款甜点不需要篝火。

### 文化融合的甜点传奇
饼干最初并非为甜点而生。1830年代，美国长老会牧师西尔维斯特·格雷厄姆发明了饼干，他认为以全谷物为中心的简单饮食能促进更健康、更美德的生活，甜点显然不是目标。讽刺的是，他启发的微甜饼干却成为了美国最奢侈甜点的基础。抱歉，格雷厄姆牧师，这恐怕不是您的初衷。

棉花糖的起源最为古老。超过2000年前，古埃及人将棉花糖植物的树脂与蜂蜜混合制成一种嚼劲大的糖果，通常仅为皇室和宗教仪式所用。这种植物也因其药用价值而备受推崇，用于缓解喉咙痛等疾病。

我们如今烤制的蓬松棉花糖直到19世纪法国糖果匠重新设计才出现，他们用打发的糖浆混合物取代了劳动密集的树脂，并将其命名为“guimauve糊”。幸运的是，这让棉花糖更易制作且价格更低廉。

巧克力的旅程始于数千年前的玛雅和阿兹特克文明，他们崇拜可可，将其制作成浓厚的苦饮。1875年，瑞士巧克力师丹尼尔·彼得成功将牛奶与巧克力混合，制成了第一块牛奶巧克力。与亨利·奈斯罗尔合作后，牛奶巧克力迅速流行起来，激励了卡多、赫舍等公司推出自己的版本。到20世纪初，价格实惠的牛奶巧克力已成为美国家庭的日常零食，并最终成为烤棉花糖的完美搭档。

将这三个故事结合，加上美国人对户外活动的热爱，便诞生了超越甜点的美味。

### 创新与传统的平衡
经典棉花糖火焰的魅力依旧。饼干、巧克力和烤棉花糖的组合难以超越。但我们也不乏创新：花生酱巧克力、美食棉花糖（从咸焦糖到浓缩咖啡风味）、甚至用饼干、华夫饼或甜甜圈代替饼干。我个人尝试过用奥利奥、白巧克力和托尼巧克力的黑牛奶巧克力薯片糖果。试试看吧！

然而，经过近一个世纪，原始配方仍是黄金标准。有些传统值得原封不动地保留。毕竟，如果不坏不糊，何必修理？
articles.summary:
If there were a Hall of Fame for desserts, s’mores would be a first-ballot inductee. They’re gooey and impossible to eat gracefully, and they somehow taste just as magical at a backyard fire pit in August as they do when you’re wrapped in a blanket beside a crackling bonfire in October. But for a treat that’s become a staple of childhood memories and cozy nights outdoors, most of us have no idea where it actually came from.

Well, every tradition has an origin story, and the history of s’mores is one of the most interesting and fun ones! How did graham crackers, chocolate and toasted marshmallows become the ultimate campfire combo? And after more than 100 years of gooey goodness, is the humble s’more finally getting a modern makeover? With International S’mores Day landing on Aug. 10, there’s no better excuse to find out and celebrate America’s favorite campfire dessert.

Read on for the sweet, sticky story behind the dessert that’s been bringing people together for generations.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

When were s’mores invented?

If you’ve ever balanced a marshmallow over a campfire while praying it doesn’t burst into flames, you have the Girl Scouts to thank. (Well, mostly.)

The earliest known published recipe for s’mores appeared in 1927 in Tramping and Trailing with the Girl Scouts, a handbook created to help troop leaders organize camping trips and outdoor activities. According to the guide, the recipe was called “Some More,” a fitting name considering no one stops at just one. The handbook credited Loretta Scott Crew, who made them for Girl Scouts by the campfire, with the recipe’s creation.

And the recipe was (and still is) wonderfully simple. On page 71, the original instructions read: “Toast two marshmallows over the coals to a crisp gooey state and then put them inside a graham cracker and chocolate bar sandwich. The heat of the marshmallow between the halves of the chocolate bar will melt the chocolate a bit. Though it tastes like ‘some more,’ one is really enough.”

Nearly 100 years later, not much has changed, although spoiler alert: The last part didn’t exactly age well.

When did this concept really take off?

Like the best trends, s’mores didn’t explode overnight—they slowly caught fire. (Pun fully intended.) The 1927 Girl Scout handbook introduced the recipe to campers across the country, but it was the post–World War II camping boom that transformed s’mores from a niche campfire snack into a national obsession. As families embraced road trips, national parks, summer camps and backyard cookouts throughout the 1940s and 1950s, millions of Americans were suddenly spending evenings around campfires with all the right ingredients nearby.

The rise of packaged graham crackers, marshmallows and chocolate bars also made the dessert incredibly easy to recreate. Companies like Hershey’s and Kraft promoted these ingredients as camping staples, while summer camps helped create generations of lifelong s’mores fans. By the late 20th century, s’mores had become less of a recipe and more of an American tradition.

Fast-forward to today, and more than 2.5 million Americans enjoy s’mores each year, according to the latest Hershey’s S’mores Heated Debate Report. What began as a simple campfire treat has become a full-blown flavor phenomenon, inspiring everything from cereal and Pop-Tarts to cookies, ice cream, coffee creamers and even s’mores chocolate mousse.

Was there anything similar to s’mores before this?

As iconic as s’mores are, the idea of pairing marshmallows with chocolate wasn’t entirely new. One of the closest predecessors arrived in 1913, when Nabisco introduced Mallomars. These chocolate-coated cookies combined a graham cracker–style cookie base with fluffy marshmallow, creating a very familiar flavor combination. The biggest difference? No campfire required.

There were also chocolate-covered marshmallow candies and homemade marshmallow desserts floating around in the early 1900s. Graham crackers had already been popular for decades, and chocolate was becoming increasingly affordable and accessible. The Girl Scouts simply combined three beloved ingredients into one brilliantly simple dessert.

Why are s’mores a uniquely American treat?

S’mores may be one of the most American desserts ever created—not just because they were invented here, but because they’re practically a culinary melting pot. Here’s a historical rundown.

Graham crackers

Believe it or not, graham crackers weren’t created with dessert in mind. They were invented in the 1830s by American Presbyterian minister Sylvester Graham, who believed a simple diet centered around whole grains would encourage healthier—and more virtuous—living. Sweet treats definitely weren’t the goal.

Ironically, the mildly sweet cracker he inspired became the foundation for one of America’s most indulgent desserts. Sorry, Reverend Graham. We don’t think this is what you had in mind.

Marshmallows

Marshmallows have one of the oldest origin stories of any s’mores ingredient. More than 2,000 years ago, ancient Egyptians mixed sap from the marshmallow plant with honey to create a chewy confection that was typically reserved for royalty and religious ceremonies. The plant was also prized for its medicinal properties and used to soothe sore throats and other ailments.

The pillowy marshmallows we roast today didn’t appear until French confectioners reinvented the candy in the 1800s, replacing the labor-intensive plant sap with whipped sugar mixtures and naming it pâte de guimauve. Thankfully for campers everywhere, they also became much easier, and cheaper, to make.

Chocolate

Chocolate’s journey started thousands of years ago with the Maya and Aztec peoples, who revered cacao and drank it as a rich, often bitter beverage long before it became dessert.

The game-changing moment came in 1875, when Swiss chocolatier Daniel Peter figured out how to blend milk with chocolate, creating the first successful milk chocolate bar. After partnering with Henri Nestlé, milk chocolate quickly exploded in popularity, inspiring companies like Cadbury and Hershey to create their own versions. By the early 1900s, affordable milk chocolate bars had become an everyday treat in American households—and eventually the perfect partner for a toasted marshmallow.

Put those three stories together, throw in America’s love affair with the great outdoors and you get something that’s far more than just dessert.

Are s’mores changing anytime soon?

Classic s’mores aren’t going anywhere. There’s something about the original trio of graham cracker, chocolate and toasted marshmallow that’s hard to improve upon.

That said, we certainly aren’t afraid to experiment! Peanut butter cups regularly replace plain chocolate bars, gourmet marshmallows come in flavors from salted caramel to espresso, and people swap graham crackers for cookies, waffles or even doughnuts. Personally, I’ve swapped milk chocolate with cookies and cream, white chocolate, and Tony’s Chocolonely’s dark milk chocolate pretzel toffee. (Give it a try and let me know what you think!)

Still, after nearly a century, the original recipe remains the gold standard. Some traditions are worth keeping exactly as they are. After all, if it isn’t broken, or deliciously gooey, why fix it?

Sources:

  • The National Confectioners Association: “Marshmallows”
  • The Hershey Company: “Hershey’s and Patrick Renna Spark Nationwide Debate Over How to Make the Perfect S’more”

articles.title: This Is the Most Dangerous Bathing Suit Color to Wear While Swimming—And It’s Probably Not the One You’re Thinking
articles.content:
让我们谈谈游泳服的颜色选择。当你购买游泳服时，你可能会考虑几件事：合身度、功能性（确保游泳时不脱落）以及流行趋势和喜欢的颜色。然而，有一件事你可能没有考虑到，但确实需要注意：选择正确的游泳服颜色不仅能让你更显身材，还能提高水中的安全性，尤其是带孩子游泳时。

根据美国疾病控制与预防中心（CDC）的数据，溺水是1至4岁儿童死亡的首要原因，并继续是儿童成长后的主要死因之一。美国游泳学校协会（USSSA）的执行主任Lisa Zarda指出，5至14岁儿童中有40%的溺水事故发生在自然水域（如湖泊、河流和海洋）。当然，溺水并非仅限于儿童。CDC还报告称，美国每年有超过4500例成人非故意溺水死亡，以及8000例非致命性溺水事件导致急诊室就医。

确保游泳安全的主要措施包括：参加游泳课程、在适当情况下佩戴美国海岸警卫队认证的救生衣、在救生员监管区域内游泳、与他人结伴游泳并注意相关警示标志。专家们强调这些协议的重要性。但除此之外，游泳服的颜色也能起到一定作用。选择正确的颜色可以增加你在水中的可见度，在紧急情况下，这可能决定生死。虽然提高可见度不能完全避免溺水，但它可以成为管理潜在风险的有效工具之一。

根据2019年水安全咨询公司Alive Solutions的研究报告，浅色系（如绿色、蓝色和白色）及“水色”系（如深蓝色和黑色）是最难以区分的颜色，无论在泳池、湖泊、海洋还是河流中，无论是水面还是水下。这意味着救生员、家人或旁观者可能难以及时发现问题。

为了在水中增加可见度，选择亮色！特别是荧光橙色和黄色，它们在不同的水域环境中最容易被发现。USSSA的Zarda表示，增加可见度在“秒数决定生死”的情况下可以起到关键作用。

Alive Solutions的报告分析了三种不同的水域环境：浅底泳池、深底泳池和开放水域。结果显示，荧光橙色和黄色在所有环境中都是最显眼的颜色。

然而，一旦水面有波浪或涟漪，几乎所有颜色在水下都会变得难以辨认。Alive Solutions调查了不同颜色的水面和水下（18英寸深）的可见度。即使在平静的水中，18英寸深处的颜色也非常难以看清。专家Tom Griffiths将水中的微波比作“浴室玻璃门或窗户上的模糊效果”。同样，浅底泳池也难以在水中观察到明亮的颜色。因此，游泳服颜色的选择不能成为防溺水的唯一手段。

Zarda建议：“穿亮色荧光游泳服是个好主意。孩子们在水下穿荧光颜色的游泳服更容易被看见，而不会与泳池底部或水中反光混为一谈。”此外，别忘了给孩子佩戴救生衣。Griffiths强调这一点：“我们绝对建议使用美国海岸警卫队认证的救生衣。救生衣不会失效，但父母和救生员可能会因为看到了他们期望看到的而失误，而我们并没有训练如何发现溺水者。”

现在让我们揭穿一个迷思：虽然许多人认为亮色会吸引鲨鱼，但穿黄色游泳服并不会增加被鲨鱼攻击的风险。这一说法源于二战时期，美国海军认为救生衣的橙色和黄色可能增加了被鲨鱼攻击的几率。经过几十年的研究，科学家发现鲨鱼并没有“美味黄色”的现象，而是对视觉对比更敏感。因此，在海洋中游泳时，应该避免高对比、高图案的游泳服。带条纹或明暗交替图案的游泳服可能很漂亮，但会增加被鲨鱼注意的风险。同样的道理适用于白色图案（如格纹）在深色背景上的游泳服。

大多数鲨鱼是色盲，但它们对颜色对比非常敏感。除了选择低对比游泳服外，专家还建议在海滩上留下珠宝和手表。在海洋中，这些闪亮的物品可能会反射光线，类似于鱼鳞，从而增加被鲨鱼注意的风险。不过，被鲨鱼攻击的概率极低，这是让游泳更安全的小建议之一。
articles.summary:
Let’s have a moment of real talk, shall we? When you’re shopping for swimsuits, there are probably a few things on your mind. There’s the fit, of course. (Hey, we’ve all got to serve.) Then there’s functionality, so it stays on when you’re swimming, running after your kids or getting pummeled by waves. And finally, there’s style and color—which is largely about this year’s trends and your favorite hues, respectively.

Well, there’s another thing that’s probably not on your mind but absolutely should be. The “right” bathing-suit color should go beyond faves and flattering choices. In fact, choosing wisely can increase your safety in the water, something that’s doubly true if you have children, while choosing poorly can do the opposite.

How, exactly? And is this more of a factor in pools, lakes or the vast ocean with its rip currents and (gulp!) sharks? To find out, we examined the latest data and talked to Tom Griffiths, a decades-long aquatic safety expert and consultant, and Lisa Zarda, executive director of the U.S. Swim School Association (USSSA). You’ll definitely want to read this before you head back into the water.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more summer safety, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

What is the main danger when it comes to water activities?

Drowning. It’s the No. 1 cause of death for children ages 1 to 4, according to the CDC, and it remains a leading cause of death for children as they age into adulthood. Zarda notes that 40% of drownings among children 5 to 14 occur in natural water (versus all sources, which includes swimming pools, hot tubs and bathtubs). And, of course, drowning is not limited to children. The CDC also reports that there are more than 4,500 unintentional fatal adult drownings each year in the U.S., plus an additional 8,000 nonfatal incidents that bring people to the emergency room.

Proper swim safety mostly entails taking swimming lessons, wearing a Coast Guard–approved life vest when appropriate, staying within lifeguard zones, swimming in groups and paying attention to important signs. The experts I spoke with emphasize those protocols most of all. But beyond that, the color of your swimsuit can make a difference. This is more than just an interesting fact: This simple choice can increase your visibility in the water, which can make a critical difference when you’re in trouble and time is of the essence. And while an increase in visibility shouldn’t be confused with a decrease in drowning, it can be a powerful tool in managing potential risks by using all of the options at your disposal.

What are the most dangerous bathing suit colors?

Light colors, like greens, blues and white, as well as “water” colors, like darker blues and blacks. That’s because these colors either reflect the surrounding colors or have low surface visibility and don’t create enough of a contrast with water. In other words, they blend into water environments more than others, which can decrease their visibility—and, as a result, yours.

In 2019, water-safety consulting company Alive Solutions produced an often-cited report suggesting these palettes are the most difficult to discern from your surroundings, regardless of the underlying pool, lake, ocean or river color, and regardless of whether they’re on the surface of the water or beneath it. That means a lifeguard, family member or bystander may not notice anything is amiss until it’s too late.

What are the safest bathing suit colors?

To increase your visibility in the water, go bright! Neon colors, especially orange and yellow, can be the easiest to spot in different aquatic settings. And increasing visibility can “make a difference [when] seconds count,” according to Zarda.

In Alive Solutions’ report, the group looked at three different conditions: light-bottomed swimming pools, dark-bottomed swimming pools and open water. It concluded that neon oranges and yellows were the most visible colors in all the different settings.

However, add in some rough water or ripples and almost any color can become very difficult to see under the surface of the water. Alive Solutions looked at both the surface visibility of the different colors and the visibility at 18 inches below the water. Even in calm water, it’s extremely difficult to see colors at the 18-inch depth, says Griffiths, who compares wavelets in water to an “obscuring bathroom glass door or an obscuring bathroom window.” The same is true of a white-bottomed pool, he adds, noting it’s very difficult to see bright colors under the water when there is any turbulence. So, again, this shouldn’t be your only line of defense when it comes to drowning—for you or your kids.

Still, says Zarda, “it is a good idea to wear a bright neon colored swimsuit. It can be easier to see kids underwater if they are wearing bright neon colors that don’t blend in with the pool bottom or light colors that could get lost in water reflections.”

And don’t forget a life jacket for kids. Griffiths remains firm on that point. “We absolutely urge the use of Coast Guard–approved life jackets,” he says. “Life jackets don’t fail, but parents and lifeguards fail because they see what they want to see, they see what they expect to see, and we don’t get any practice at detecting drowning victims.”

Hold on—isn’t “yum-yum yellow” really attractive to sharks?

Let’s do some myth-busting! Although there’s a widely held belief that bright colors attract sharks because of their high visibility in the ocean to human eyes, wearing a yellow suit does not actually increase your risk of a shark attack.

According to the BBC, the idea that “yum-yum yellow” is a shark favorite probably got its start sometime in World War II, when the U.S. Navy dealt with its fair share of shark attacks. These men came to believe that the oranges and yellows associated with life preservers increased their comrades’ chances of being targeted by sharks. This anecdotal evidence led to some pretty deep scientific inquiry into the makeup of sharks’ eyes over the next few decades, and the truth is that there isn’t really a “yum-yum yellow” phenomenon. Instead, it’s more likely that the yellow worn by some of the men created more visual contrast for sharks. And contrast, it turns out, is the critical factor to avoid when it comes to these toothy sea dwellers.

And yes, that means there are certain kinds of suits you should avoid for ocean swimming. They just might not all be yellow.

What is the most dangerous bathing suit color when it comes to shark bites?

To decrease attention from sharks, skip the high-contrast, highly patterned suits. Stripes may be cute, but avoid patterns that alternate light and dark striping. The same goes for the sweet white patterns—like gingham—on darker backgrounds. Cool for the pool, but maybe a little too attractive to a shark.

The thing is, many species of sharks are colorblind. But being colorblind doesn’t mean they can’t see color contrast. In fact, they can be extremely good at that! Beyond choosing a low-contrast suit, experts also recommend leaving your jewelry and watches on the sand. In the ocean, these shiny objects can reflect light the same way fish scales do, creating more of a danger when it comes to sharks.

We should also note that your risk of being attacked by a shark is extremely low. Still, this is another piece of information that can make it just a little safer to go back in the water.

Sources:

  • Tom Griffiths, PhD, water-safety consultant for the Aquatic Safety Research Group and professor emeritus; phone interview, July 14, 2026
  • Lisa Zarda, executive director of the United States Swim School Association; email interview, July 15, 2026
  • Lehigh Valley Health Network: “Shopping for Children’s Swimsuits? Keep Color in Mind”
  • BBC: “‘Yum-yum yellow’: Could your swimwear attract sharks?”
  • Alive Solutions: “All Things Aquatic + Water Safety”
  • Florida Museum: “Yearly Worldwide Shark Attack Summary”
  • Florida Museum: “Advice to Swimmers”
  • Florida Museum: “Color of Apparel”

articles.title: You Won’t Believe How They Made the Cyclops in The Odyssey (Hint: It Involved a 60-Foot Puppet)
articles.content: In the new Christopher Nolan movie The Odyssey, soldiers from the Greek island of Ithaca end up trapped in a cave with a terrifying, enormous creature. The blockbuster film loosely follows the legendary poem by Homer, and students of Greek history will recognize the one-eyed giant Cyclops. Odysseus, the Greek king played by Matt Damon, who is trying to make it home to his wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway) and their son, encounters many strange creatures on his decades-long journey. However, the Cyclops stands out for his size and the frightening scene in which the soldiers slip out of the cave camouflaged as a herd of sheep as the monster sleeps. But how was the creature created? That’s an interesting story all by itself. According to NBC News, Nolan used a 60-foot puppet to create the Cyclops, whose formal name is Polyphemus in Greek mythology. Actor Bill Irwin, who previously played the robot in Nolan’s Interstellar, brought the Cyclops to life. The filmmakers created the fiction that the Cyclops was interacting with soldiers by also filming footage of Irwin at Nestor’s Cave, a limestone cavern with ties to ancient mythology in Messenia, Greece. Nolan avoided using CGI or a green screen. Instead, he used animatronics, puppetry and computer graphics. He wanted the monster to have complexity and seem realistic, so it was also important to him to have a real actor play the character. Nolan revealed that creating the Cyclops was one of the toughest things he’s done as a director. Nolan didn’t want the Cyclops to seem like a cartoon. “Everything about the Cyclops sequence is aimed at trying to imagine: What would this be like in real life?” Nolan told Empire. “Not approaching it from a storybook or cartoony point of view, but really trying to be in there with Odysseus and his men. It’s a horrifying situation.” Damon revealed in the interview with Empire that shooting the scene was difficult because thousands of bees hovered at the cave door. The filmmakers used 40 real sheep to film the scene, and Nolan explained that it felt more realistic to film the scene in a real cave. Nolan told podcaster Jake Stakes that he was trying to give people a “reason to believe” the character was real. He said going to real places was key to making Cyclops come to life. “We used every trick in the book,” Nolan said. Add Reader’s Digest on Google! A puppet and a real actor brought the Cyclops to life

According to NBC News, Nolan used a 60-foot puppet to create the Cyclops, whose formal name is Polyphemus in Greek mythology. The filmmakers created the fiction that the Cyclops was interacting with soldiers by also filming footage of Irwin at Nestor’s Cave, a limestone cavern with ties to ancient mythology in Messenia, Greece.

Nolan avoided using CGI or a green screen. Instead, he used animatronics, puppetry and computer graphics. He wanted the monster to have complexity and seem realistic, so it was also important to him to have a real actor play the character.

Nolan says he didn’t want the monster to be a cartoon

Nolan didn’t want the Cyclops to seem like a cartoon.

“Everything about the Cyclops sequence is aimed at trying to imagine: What would this be like in real life?” Nolan told Empire. “Not approaching it from a storybook or cartoony point of view, but really trying to be in there with Odysseus and his men. It’s a horrifying situation.”

Damon revealed in the interview with Empire that shooting the scene was difficult because thousands of bees hovered at the cave door. The filmmakers used 40 real sheep to film the scene, and Nolan explained that it felt more realistic to film the scene in a real cave.

“We used every trick in the book,” Nolan said.

articles.title: No, You’re Not Hallucinating—There’s a Decimal Point on That Speed Limit Sign. Here’s Why
articles.content:
Speed limit signs can either fade into the background or startle us to attention, often depending on how fast we might be going. Familiarity plays a role too. We expect to see 25 mph in a quiet residential neighborhood and 55 or 65 mph on a busy highway. But what if you were driving along and saw 8.2 mph, or 14.4? Most speedometers don’t even display tenths of a mile per hour, so how is a driver supposed to follow a rule of the road like that?
It sounds ridiculous, and it is a bit uncommon, but speed limits expressed in decimals definitely do exist. To explain what’s going on, Reader’s Digest reached out to Michael Knodler, PhD, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and the director of the UMass Transportation Center. Read on to find out the purpose behind these unusual speed limits and whether they might soon appear on a road near you.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more travel, tech, cleaning, humor and fun facts all week long.
Speed restrictions date all the way back to the days of non-motorized transportation, though they were a little more loosely defined. As far back as 1652, officials in what was then known as New Amsterdam—now New York City—declared that no wagons, carts or sleighs “shall be run, rode or driven at a gallop,” according to History.com.
With the arrival and proliferation of the automobile in America in the late 19th century, formal speed limits soon followed. Connecticut is widely credited as the first state to enact an official automobile speed limit in May 1901, setting a maximum speed of 12 mph in cities and 15 mph on country roads. The most important provision? Drivers had to slow down or even stop when encountering horse-drawn vehicles so that they wouldn’t startle the horses.
Automobiles continued to improve and become faster as time wore on, but there were no official national speed limits in the United States until much later. In January 1974, President Richard Nixon, responding to the oil crisis and skyrocketing fuel costs, signed legislation that established 55 mph as the maximum speed allowed nationwide. That federal limit stood until 1995, when authority for setting speed limits was returned to states and local jurisdictions.
Today, speed limits vary from place to place. The Federal Highway Administration notes that some common limits include 25 mph in residential or school districts, 55 mph on rural highways and 65 to 70 mph on rural interstate highways. The highest posted speed limit in the country is 85 mph, found on a stretch of Texas State Highway 130.
There are two main reasons jurisdictions or property owners might post odd speed limits like this, according to Knodler.
The idea gained attention when drivers in Appleton, Wisconsin, were recently greeted with a 17.3 mph speed limit at the Outagamie Country Recycling and Solid Waste Facility. According to a Facebook post introducing the new speed limit and sign to the public, safety was the No. 1 reason for the new eye-catching speed limit.
The effectiveness of these types of speed limits remains a bit of a question mark, according to Knodler.
Most research on unique speed limits hasn’t focused on those with decimal points, in part because they are not technically supposed to be used on public roads. “The evidence to date would be mostly anecdotal, but it would be easy enough to study if there was interest,” he says.
One thing that is clear, however: Any measure that encourages drivers to pay closer attention behind the wheel can be a positive step in the direction of creating safer roads.
Official statements about decimal speed limits are scarce, but signs with unusual speed limits are often found in semi-private residential developments, private properties and other areas where property owners may install their own traffic signs, even if they don’t necessarily comply with roadway standards.
“It’s really a bit of a gray area,” Knodler says, explaining that the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices is the federal standard and requires speed limits posted on roads that “are inviting of the public”—including some seemingly private areas such as condominium complexes—need to meet certain requirements. They must be based upon an engineering study, be in increments of 5 mph and be displayed on a white regulatory sign with black letters.
So why do these signs continue to appear in places when they don’t meet those requirements? “There are plenty of examples of noncompliant traffic control devices everywhere,” Knodler says. “I joke that I give my students an assignment every year to go out and find a noncompliant TCD, and it is the easiest assignment because they all get 100%.”
For now, these signs remain a curiosity more than anything. Official traffic signs are strictly regulated, and the likelihood of widespread adoption is slim. Still, says Knodler, “they are fun, and, as mentioned, attention grabbing.”
